strengths: Novel and elegant theoretical contribution: an exact factorization of the GFT basis into localized subgraph GFTs composed with Cauchy factors (Theorem 3.1), generalizing rank-one update results from Fernández-Menduiña et al. (2025) to arbitrary symmetric matrices and arbitrary partitions, with the repeated-eigenvalue/orthogonality edge cases handled via deflation (Section C).

Quadratic-time complexity result (Theorem 3.2, O(kn^2)) is clearly derived, with the complexity analysis in the appendix carefully accounting for the hierarchical merge structure, and it is empirically validated on synthetic graphs (Figure 2 confirms quadratic scaling; Figure 3 confirms linear scaling in interface size k).

The paper goes beyond the factorization itself: a greedy partitioning algorithm directly optimized for the theoretical factorization cost (Eq. 7) and a principled use of localized spectral sparsification (Theorem 4.1) with a Lipschitz-filter perturbation argument connecting it to L2G-Net layers.

Empirical evaluation on a modern, well-regarded heterophilous benchmark (Platonov et al., 2023) with a broad baseline comparison (Table 5), showing competitive performance (best on Minesweeper) with substantially fewer parameters than transformer baselines, plus an interpretable Grad-CAM analysis (Figure 5) supporting the locality claim.

Reproducibility is reasonably strong: full hyperparameter tables, sparsification details (effective-resistance sampling, LOBPCG Fiedler vectors, JL projections), and detailed pseudocode (Algorithms 1-3) are provided.
weaknesses: The central 'local-to-global hierarchical' narrative is only weakly exercised in practice: the real-world experiments use a single level of hierarchy (one partition into two subgraphs), so the full divide-and-conquer machinery that motivates the theory is essentially untested on real data; only the synthetic experiments probe deeper hierarchies.

The factorization is exact only for the sparsified graph, not the original: with sparsification ratios retaining as little as 0.5% of interface edges, the claimed speedups partly reflect computing the eigendecomposition of a different graph, and the quality impact of this approximation is only indirectly assessed through downstream accuracy.

No analysis of numerical stability of the deep chain of Cauchy factors: repeated rank-one updates via secular-equation solvers are known to be delicate, and error accumulation across k(2^L - 1) updates in float precision is not analyzed or measured (e.g., orthogonality drift of U(Phi)).

Missing comparison against natural alternatives for obtaining spectral bases (e.g., Lanczos/partial eigendecomposition, or recently proposed fast GFT approximations) at matched accuracy; Table 2 compares only against dense eigendecomposition, which is a weak baseline for runtime.

Empirical wins over the strongest baselines are modest: Polynormer outperforms L2G-Net on 3 of 4 datasets (e.g., 54.81 vs 53.41 on Amazon-ratings, 85.91 vs 85.57 on Tolokers), so 'competitive with state-of-the-art' is accurate but the advantage rests mainly on parameter count and interpretability rather than accuracy.

The claimed 'orders of magnitude fewer parameters' is only visualized in Figure 4 without exact parameter counts or training wall-clock times reported in tables; end-to-end training cost (not just preprocessing) is not reported.

Some presentational and consistency issues: sign discrepancy between Eq. (5) and Theorem D.1 (U^T~ = D(λ~,λ)U^T vs. -D(λ~,λ)U^T), Theorem 4.1 is essentially a re-application of Spielman-Srivastava with limited independent novelty, and there is no explicit limitations section (limitations are scattered across Sections 4.2 and 6).

General applicability is unclear for graphs lacking community structure, where the greedy partitioning may yield leaves everywhere and L2G-Net reduces to a standard global GFT plus sparsification; the paper asserts graceful degradation but provides limited evidence beyond the four benchmarks.

strengths: The core idea is interesting and well-motivated: connecting rank-one eigenvalue-update theory (secular equations, orthogonal Cauchy-like matrices) to graph partitions yields an exact factorization of the GFT basis, which is a clean and non-obvious construction that generalizes Fernández-Menduiña et al. (2025) from path graphs to arbitrary symmetric matrices/graphs.

The theoretical development is careful: the deflation treatment of repeated eigenvalues and orthogonal updates (Section C, Appendix D) addresses the corner cases that the prior rank-one-update analysis glossed over, and the complexity analysis (Theorem 3.2, Appendix E) is carried out in detail for sequential and parallel solvers.

The synthetic experiments (Figures 2 and 3) directly validate the predicted O(kn^2) scaling in both graph size and interface size, and the preprocessing overhead is shown to be negligible, which supports the central complexity claim.

The interface sparsification analysis (Theorem 4.1) with Laplacian quadratic-form guarantees and a Lipschitz-based filter perturbation argument gives a principled handle on the approximation that the GNN experiments actually rely on.
The localization analysis (Section 6.3, Figure 5) is a nice interpretability experiment that empirically supports the claimed local-to-global inductive bias.
weaknesses: The practical payoff is much smaller than the framing suggests. Table 2 shows the Cauchy factorization is only ~2.2-3x faster than a dense eigendecomposition (e.g., 232s vs. 731s on Roman-empire), not an orders-of-magnitude improvement, and the O(kn^2) cost remains prohibitive for graphs beyond ~10^5 nodes. For a paper whose headline claim is computational tractability of exact spectral methods, the demonstrated regime is narrow.

The real-world evaluation undermines the paper's own narrative. On the four heterophilous benchmarks, the model uses a single level of hierarchy and very aggressive interface sparsification (Table 4 reports k after sparsification of 1 on three of four datasets, and the text mentions up to 99.5% edge sparsification). At k=1 the 'hierarchical local-to-global' machinery is essentially unused, so it is unclear whether the empirical gains come from the factorization or merely from running a modest spectral GNN on a slightly modified graph.

The reported accuracy is not actually superior: Polynormer beats L2G-Net on Roman-empire (92.55 vs. 92.12), Amazon-ratings (54.81 vs. 53.41), and Tolokers (85.91 vs. 85.57), and GRAMAGCN beats it on Tolokers by a wide margin (86.23 vs. 85.57). The abstract's 'competitive with the state-of-the-art' is defensible but generous; the parameter-efficiency claim (Figure 4) is the only clearly supported empirical advantage.

The sparsification changes the problem: the factorization is exact for the sparsified graph, not the original. The O(epsilon) filter-deviation argument in Section 4.2 depends on Lipschitz continuity of the filters, yet the paper simultaneously uses learnable RBF/spline filters with learned centers (Appendix B.2) whose Lipschitz constants are uncontrolled. No experiment quantifies the spectral approximation error or its effect on downstream accuracy.

Novelty of the theory is incremental: Lemma 3.1 / Theorem 3.1 is a direct composition of the known rank-one update identity (Bunch et al., 1978; Golub, 1973; Fernández-Menduiña et al., 2025), the deflation procedures in Appendix C are standard numerical linear algebra, and the sparsification result in Theorem 4.1 follows almost immediately from Spielman-Srivastava. The main genuinely new material is the HGF partitioning heuristic, which is a greedy spectral-bisection scheme evaluated only on Barabási-Albert graphs.

There is no empirical comparison against the fast-GFT baselines the paper itself discusses (Le Magoarou et al., 2018; Frerix and Bruna, 2019), despite claiming quadratic complexity and lower setup cost as advantages; the complexity comparisons are also against an unoptimized numpy.linalg.eigh rather than state-of-the-art sparse eigensolvers (e.g., LOBPCG, which the authors themselves use for the Fiedler vector), inflating the apparent speedup.

Several presentation issues reduce confidence: the sign convention is inconsistent between Lemma 3.1 (U~^T = D U~^T) and Theorem D.1 (U~^T = -D U^T); Theorem 3.1's statement of the factor composition with lambda-tilde notation is confusing; and Section F promises Table 5 as 'more experimental results' but provides no analysis of it.

Reproducibility concerns: no code release is mentioned, and several important details are under-specified (e.g., how the quantile sweep over balance tolerances selects among candidate partitions, the epsilon/retention values used per dataset beyond Table 3, and the exact Global GFT baseline configuration used in Figures 4-5).

strengths: The core technical result is clean and useful: an exact Cauchy-matrix factorization of the graph Fourier basis for arbitrary graphs via hierarchical partitions, with an O(kn²) algorithm (Theorem 3.2), avoiding O(n³) full eigendecomposition. The synthesis of rank-one spectral update theory (Bunch et al., Golub) with graph partitioning is a genuine and original contribution to fast spectral graph algorithms.

The paper is honest about its theoretical scope: degeneracies and orthogonal-update cases are handled via a deflation procedure (Appendix C), and Theorem 4.1 gives a principled sparsification route to bound interface size rather than ad-hoc truncation.

The synthetic experiments directly validate the theoretical complexity claims: runtime scaling is quadratic in n (Figure 2) and linear in interface size k (Figure 3), with negligible preprocessing overhead, which is the right way to support a complexity-focused contribution.

On the heterophilous benchmarks (Table 5), L2G-Net is competitive with much larger attention-based models while using orders of magnitude fewer parameters (Figure 4), and consistently beats a Global GFT baseline, supporting the locality claim. The Grad-CAM analysis (Figure 5) is a nice interpretability check that predictive importance is localized.
The runtime comparison (Table 2) shows a concrete 3x speedup over full eigendecomposition on real graphs, including a dense worst case (Tolokers).
weaknesses: The empirical case for the GNN itself is thin. L2G-Net is best only on Minesweeper (97.50 vs. 97.46 for Polynormer, within noise) and trails Polynormer on the other three benchmarks (e.g., Amazon-ratings 53.41 vs. 54.81; Roman-empire 92.12 vs. 92.55). Claims like 'competitive with state-of-the-art' are defensible, but the headline framing could lead readers to overestimate the empirical advance; the more decisive contribution is the factorization algorithm, not the classifier.

Real-world experiments use only one level of hierarchy (a single two-way partition, Section 6.2), so the central 'hierarchical local-to-global' mechanism is validated mainly on synthetic graphs. The behavior of L2G-Net with deep hierarchies on real graphs (e.g., oversmoothing across levels, filter interactions across r,p) is untested.

No numerical stability analysis of the Cauchy factorization is provided. The method composes many OCLMs built from secular equations; near-degenerate eigenvalues or near-orthogonal updates are known to make these updates ill-conditioned, and graph spectra (with repeated eigenvalues, handled only via deflation) are precisely where this is a risk. No reported check that the composed basis is orthonormal or that U(Φ)ᵀ approximates the true GFT basis within tolerance.

There is a sign inconsistency between Lemma 3.1 (Eq. 5, Ũᵀ = D(λ̃,λ)Uᵀ) and Theorem D.1 in the appendix (Eq. 25, Ũᵀ = −D(λ̃,λ)Uᵀ), and the definition of D already contains a minus sign. This should be reconciled.

The claimed robustness 'even with up to 99.5% edge sparsification' is not backed by an ablation: only the final sparsified configurations are reported (Table 4), with no curve showing accuracy vs. sparsification ratio, which is the key practical trade-off of the method.

The factorization cost is a preprocessing cost amortized over training, but its magnitude is nontrivial (232–896 s, Table 2) and must be redone if the graph or sparsification level changes; scalability beyond the ~25k-node regime of the benchmark (where full ED is still feasible) is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The HGF construction (Section 4.1) relies on a greedy heuristic with an accept/reject criterion (Eq. 7) whose sensitivity to the Fiedler-vector bisection and quantile sweep is not analyzed; behavior on graphs without community structure is only touched upon indirectly.

No code release or reproducibility statement is included, despite a fairly intricate pipeline (partitioning, LOBPCG, JL-based resistance estimation, secular-equation solvers, filter banks) that would be hard to reimplement exactly.

strengths: Novel and well-executed connection between classical divide-and-conquer eigensolver theory (rank-one updates, Cauchy-like matrices, secular equations) and graph neural networks. The exact Cauchy factorization of the GFT (Theorem 3.1) with O(kn^2) complexity scaled by cut size is a clean, provable result that enables exact spectral processing without full eigendecomposition.

The theoretical development is thorough: the paper extends prior rank-one-update results (Fernandez-Menduina et al., 2025a) to arbitrary symmetric matrices, handles repeated eigenvalues and orthogonal updates via deflation (Appendix D), and proves both the factorization and an expressiveness result (L2G-Net strictly contains global spectral filters) with a minimal explicit counterexample.

Runtime scaling claims are empirically validated on synthetic graphs (quadratic in n, linear in cut size), and the method is demonstrated to make exact spectral processing tractable at a scale where full eigendecomposition is infeasible (569k-node London graph factorized in ~144 minutes, three-four orders of magnitude faster than the extrapolated ED runtime).

Comprehensive evaluation across transductive heterophilous benchmarks (Platonov et al.), long-range inductive benchmarks (peptides-func/struct), and large-scale City-Networks, with the method competitive with or better than strong spectral baselines using orders of magnitude fewer parameters.

Additional supporting analyses strengthen the case: memory savings (Table 5), end-to-end training times and per-epoch costs (Tables 10-11), Grad-CAM localization study demonstrating the local-to-global inductive bias, and learned filter visualizations showing task adaptation.

Honest about scope: the conclusion acknowledges that polynomial filters/message passing remain preferable when linear complexity is key, and the paper is transparent that sparsification is an approximation applied to cuts.
weaknesses: Novelty is partly incremental relative to the well-established divide-and-conquer eigensolver literature (Cuppen, Bunch et al., Gu-Eisenstat); the core machinery is a generalization of known rank-one update identities, with the novelty residing in the graph-theoretic framing (cut-size complexity) and the GNN application. The paper does articulate the differences, but reviewers may judge the algorithmic contribution as modest on its own.

Empirical accuracy gains are modest: on the Platonov benchmarks the method is competitive but does not consistently beat Polynormer (loses on Roman-empire 92.12 vs 92.55 and Amazon-ratings 53.39 vs 54.81), and on peptides-struct it is worse than plain GCN (0.2479 vs 0.2460). The strongest quantitative claim is parameter efficiency rather than accuracy.

The per-epoch cost is quadratic and often higher than baselines (e.g., 1.54 s/epoch on Roman-empire vs 0.48 for Polynormer), and end-to-end training is sometimes slower (50:03 vs 28:56 on Roman-empire), so the practical efficiency claim is nuanced and depends on the regime.

The 'exactness' of the factorization applies to the (possibly sparsified) graph; since cut sparsification is used whenever cuts are large (e.g., Tolokers retains 25 edges after sparsification), the method on real graphs often computes the GFT of an approximation. The error is bounded via spectral sparsification guarantees, but the downstream effect of this approximation on learned filters is analyzed only via Lipschitz-type arguments rather than directly measured.

Numerical stability of chaining many Cauchy factors is not deeply analyzed. Near-degenerate eigenvalues are common (Figure 7), and while deflation handles degeneracies, error accumulation across long factor chains for deep hierarchies (L=6 on London) is not quantified (e.g., reconstruction error of U against the true basis).

The greedy HGF construction (Section 4.1) is a heuristic without approximation guarantees on the achieved cost, and synthetic validation is limited to Barabasi-Albert graphs; robustness of the partitioning pipeline on other graph families is not shown.

Some presentation issues: the main-text proof sketch of Theorem 4.1 leans on applying spectral sparsification 'independently to each interface' without fully justifying composition across levels; Table 1's complexity comparison is somewhat generous (L2G-Net's forward pass is O(n^2), comparable to graph transformers).

strengths: The core idea of connecting rank-one Laplacian updates (edge insertions) to Cauchy-type eigenbasis rotations is elegant, and packaging divide-and-conquer eigensolver machinery (Cuppen 1980; Gu & Eisenstat 1995) as a graph-structured GFT factorization with locality semantics is a genuinely interesting reframing for the GNN community.

The experimental coverage is broad and mostly well-designed: synthetic runtime scaling experiments validating the O(kn^2) claim, heterophilous benchmarks (Platonov et al.), inductive LRGB peptides tasks, and very large City-Networks graphs where full eigendecomposition is infeasible (memory and runtime tables on factorization alone are convincing).

The paper is honest about positioning: it explicitly concedes that message passing remains preferable for linear-complexity regimes, discusses deflation for repeated/near-degenerate eigenvalues (Figure 7), and provides interpretability analyses (learned filters, Grad-CAM localization) supporting the locality claim.
Expressiveness result (Theorem 5.1) with a clean minimal counterexample showing L2G-Net strictly contains global spectral filters is a nice touch.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to the numerical linear algebra literature: the central factorization is essentially Cuppen/Gu-Eisenstat divide-and-conquer eigensolving via rank-one updates and secular equations. The claimed distinctions in Appendix B (input is graph-sparse; output is a factorization rather than the eigendecomposition) are overstated - D&C solvers already compute exactly this implicit orthogonal factorization, and the deflation treatment of repeated eigenvalues follows Bunch et al. (1978) almost directly.

Soundness gap in the main complexity result: Theorem 3.2 claims O(kn^2 + sum f_i(n)), but the proof in Appendix F derives O(kn^2 + k^2 n (L^2 log n - L^3)) with the fast Cauchy product, and explicitly notes an O(k^2 n^2) bound with a quadratic product, only to argue the true behavior 'has been observed' to be O(kn^2) empirically. An empirical observation cannot substitute for the missing proof of the headline bound.

Theorem 4.1 appears incorrect as stated: the interface sparsification claim k' <= O(eps^{-2}) is independent of the original interface size k and the subgraph sizes, with no justification from Spielman-Srivastava-style analysis (which typically yields bounds scaling with the number of vertices, e.g., O(n' log n / eps^2)). As written, the guarantee does not follow from the cited result.

The headline empirical claim is 'competitive', not superior: L2G-Net loses to Polynormer on 3 of 4 Platonov benchmarks and is mid-pack on peptides (peptides-struct MAE is worse than many GNN baselines). The parameter-efficiency selling point (Figure 5) does not fully offset the absence of clear accuracy wins, especially given the added per-graph preprocessing (partitioning, sparsification, secular solves).

Practical deployment concerns are under-addressed: the architecture is fixed by the graph before training (transductive by construction); for inductive tasks the paper only uses L=1 on small peptides graphs, sidestepping the question of how the hierarchy generalizes to unseen graphs. Numerical stability of chaining many Cauchy factors across levels (L up to 6 on 569k nodes) is discussed qualitatively but not rigorously error-bounded.

Asymptotic advantage over graph transformers is thin: Table 1 lists L2G-Net as O(kn^2) versus GT O(n^2), which for the k = O(1) regimes the method targets is only a constant-factor difference, undermining the framing of the complexity comparison.

Reproducibility is uncertain: hyperparameters are documented, but no code release is mentioned, and the pipeline involves several nontrivial components (quantile-swept spectral bisection, JL-approximated effective resistances, deflation, secular equation solving) that would be difficult to reimplement reliably.

strengths: The core idea is elegant and well-grounded in classical numerical linear algebra: leveraging the rank-one-update eigenvector identity (Bunch et al., 1978; Cuppen 1980) to obtain an *exact* Cauchy/OCLM factorization of the GFT basis for any hierarchical graph partition, with localized factors tied to bridge edges.

The complexity analysis is careful and honest: O(kn²) with dependence on the cut size k rather than edge count, and the paper explicitly characterizes when the method is unfavorable (k = O(n)). The sparsification result (Theorem 4.1) gives a principled fallback with (1±ε) spectral guarantees.

Theoretical claims are backed by a full derivation in the appendix, including the deflation machinery for repeated/near-degenerate eigenvalues, and an expressiveness result (Theorem 5.1) with a clean, minimal strict-containment counterexample.

The synthetic runtime experiments directly validate the predicted scaling (quadratic in n, linear in k), and the City-Networks experiments demonstrate genuine practical value: factorizing a 569k-node graph in ~144 minutes where full eigendecomposition OOMs.

Comparison against the full-GFT baseline across accuracy, parameters, memory, and interpretability (Grad-CAM localization) is thorough and supports the claimed local-to-global inductive bias. Reproducibility is aided by detailed hyperparameter tables and algorithmic pseudocode.
weaknesses: The central mathematical identity (eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix after a rank-one update form an OCLM) is classical; the paper's novelty rests on composing it for graph partitions and inserting learnable filters. This is acknowledged, but the theoretical contribution is incremental relative to Cuppen-style divide-and-conquer eigensolvers and (Fernández-Menduiña et al., 2025a), which the paper itself positions as the direct precursor.

The 'exact factorization' claim is undermined in the empirical regime: the transductive benchmarks use only L = 1 (a single split) and very aggressive cut sparsification (e.g., 0.005 on Roman-empire/Minesweeper, i.e., retaining ~0.5% of cut edges). The factorization is exact for the *sparsified* graph, not the original; the effective approximation error incurred in the actual experiments is not quantified.

Accuracy gains are modest and often within one standard deviation of baselines: on Platonov et al. benchmarks L2G-Net trails Polynormer on three of four datasets; on peptides it is within noise of SOTA but not best; on City-Networks it does not uniformly beat Exphormer (Shanghai, LA). Headline claims such as 'outperforms existing spectral strategies' are defensible but the empirical contribution is competitive rather than clearly superior.

No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility for a method with many pipeline-specific choices (Fiedler bisection with quantile sweeps, JL-based resistance approximation, sparsification ratios, spline filter parameterization).

Numerical robustness of chaining many OCLM factors (error accumulation across k(2^L−1) sequential secular solves) is not analyzed; the eigengap analysis (Figure 7) shows near-degeneracies are common in practice, and the treatment is empirical rather than with stability bounds.

The dominant runtime comparison is against dense eigendecomposition, which is a somewhat weak strawman for very large graphs; comparisons against alternative structured/orthogonal-factorization approaches (e.g., butterfly or HSS-based solvers, which the paper cites) are absent.
Scope is limited to undirected/static graphs; this is honestly stated but narrows applicability.
